extracted.intended_audience: writers, readers, and critics of poetry and language (general literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles about poetic voice, diction, use of dialect/slang, authenticity, and the role of rawness versus polish in verse and prose. Useful for writers and critics judging or crafting poems and literary utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialect/patois as a poetic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: "His brightest hit is his use of the Scotch patois, so full of terms flavor'd like wild fruits or berries."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialect/patois can be a poet's chief asset: it supplies native spice, untranslatable twang, local color, and authenticity. Examples given: song titles and Scots lines. Advice implicit: favor retaining local terms and idiom where they add flavor rather than sanitizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for rawness/first-drafts/unfinish when authentic
rubrics_metrics.description: "His collected works in giving everything, are nearly one half first drafts... Curiously even the frequent crudeness, haste, deficiencies... prove upon the whole not out of keeping..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpolished elements—neglect, unfinish, careless nudity, slovenly hiatus—may come from intrinsic genius and can please more than overworked polish. For some poets, reproducing original, raw material preserves veracity and emotional force; do not always smooth away rough edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity/veracity of subject-matter and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "complete the full abandon and veracity of the farm-fields and the home-brew'd flavor of the Scotch vernacular."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithful representation of a milieu (farm-fields, working-class life, vernacular practices) heightens credibility and reader engagement. Match linguistic choices to lived experience portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness, 'snap', and idiomatic wit
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hardly a piece of his, large or small, but has 'snap' and raciness... much cutting irony and idiomatic ear-cuffing..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems benefit from brisk energy, crisp phrasing, idiomatic turns, and sharp irony or wit. These qualities give immediacy and make lines memorable; cultivate idiomatic speech and rhetorical 'punch' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/psychological depth beneath surface gaiety
rubrics_metrics.description: "The basis of Burns's character... was hypochondria... From such deep-down elements sprout up, in very contrast and paradox, those riant utterances of which a superficial reading will not detect the hidden foundation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful work can pair buoyant exterior tone with darker or complex undercurrents; this paradoxical depth enriches meaning and rewards close reading. Seek contrasts between surface voice and subterranean feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free, bold handling and a dominating personal voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "In these compositions... the composer reigns alone, with handling free and broad and true, and is an artist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the poet's singular personality controls the piece—free, broad, authoritative handling—the work attains artistic stature. Boldness of treatment and a clear individual presence are marks of high artistry; editions that retain such handling are often preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability to audience and the 'homely' taste
rubrics_metrics.description: "The longer and more elaborated poems... would please a natural but homely taste, and cute but average intellect, and are inimitable in their way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the intended or likely audience: some works deliberately aim at a broad, homely, or popular taste and succeed on those terms. 'Inimitable in their way' points to value in writing that perfectly fits a particular, perhaps non-elite, audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness and racy flavor over profundity
rubrics_metrics.description: "With nothing profound in any of them, what there is of moral and plot has an inimitably fresh and racy flavor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or plot simplicity can be offset by freshness of expression and vivacity. Do not require profundity as the sole measure of worth; freshness, charm, and distinct flavor are legitimate virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of diction, sound, and 'finest verbalism' (Tennyson)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To me, Tennyson shows more than any poet I know... how much there is in finest verbalism. There is such a latent charm in mere words, cunning collocutions, and in the voice ringing them..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful choice of words, collocation, and attention to sonic qualities (rhythm, resonance) can be central virtues. Valuing 'verbalism' means recognizing the power of language itself—its music and exact phrasing—as a criterion of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of personal moral/tonal line
rubrics_metrics.description: "He has been consistent throughout with the native, healthy, patriotic spinal element and promptings of himself. His moral line is local and conventional, but it is vital and genuine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer's coherence of outlook and consistent voice can be strengths; authenticity of conviction—even when conventional—adds integrity. Evaluate whether the work’s moral/tonal stance genuinely expresses the author's sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive mannerism as acceptable/valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: "His mannerism is great, but it is a noble and welcome mannerism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong stylistic mannerism, even if recognizable or repetitive, can be valuable when it is noble or fitting. Distinctive personal mannerisms should be weighed as possible assets rather than automatic faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang/indirection as a generative force for poetry and language
rubrics_metrics.description: "Slang... is the lawless germinal element, below all words and sentences, and behind all poetry... an attempt of common humanity to escape from bald literalism... which in highest walks produces poets and poems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colloquial speech, indirection, and informal turns of phrase often seed figurative language and poetic invention. Writers should attend to the creative potential of slang and indirect expression when seeking fresh metaphors or idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal coinages can become stable lexicon (word-formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Many of the oldest and solidest words we use, were originally generated from the daring and license of slang."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive or daring informal words may eventually gain permanence. Encourage experimental coinages when they illuminate sense; historical precedent shows slang frequently becomes standard vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/masses determine linguistic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Language, be it remember'd, is not an abstract construction... Its final decisions are made by the masses, people nearest the concrete..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy and staying power of words and usages depend on popular adoption. Writers and critics should observe which usages resonate with real readers rather than rely solely on prescriptive norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nicknames and colloquial naming for social authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of nicknames and local slang: "Little Mac," "Uncle Billy," state-epithets (e.g., 'Knickerbockers'), place-names like 'Whiskey Flat' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing popular nicknames, sobriquets, and colorful place-names can lend verisimilitude and social realism. Such naming practices also supply humor and character; incorporate them when they serve scene-setting or voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional slang and toponymy as a source of originality
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Western States... are... the special areas of slang... names of localities, towns, rivers..." with many cited examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regionalisms and local place-names often provide striking, original linguistic material. Using regional vocabulary and toponymy can root work in a particular geography and culture, offering freshness and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing humor and imagination from everyday speech and workers
rubrics_metrics.description: "You get more real fun from half an hour with them than from the books of all 'the American humorists.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everyday conversations of laborers, drivers, miners, etc., are fertile for authentic humor, repartee, and ephemeral imaginative sparks. Writers seeking comic or spontaneous material should observe common speech and repartee.
